Precise monthly revenue data showed July 2026 revenue of NT$100 million (approximately $3.1 million), up 20.7% year-over-year and 5.7% month-over-month, setting a new record. Full Q2 revenue was NT$270 million (approximately $8.5 million), up 22.1% year-over-year, the highest growth rate in the past five quarters. Chairman Liu Chu-Chi, responding to a question on gross margin, emphasized: "During the transition period between the old Special Regulations and the Regenerative Medicine Act last year, public willingness to undergo treatment wavered temporarily, but business has clearly recovered over the past few months."
CAR001 Phase I Data: 382-Day Complete Remission in Brain Tumor, 72.8% Shrinkage in Colorectal Cancer
The most compelling segment of the earnings call was Liu Chu-Chi's personal account of CAR001 Phase I case results. Among 15 subjects, one end-stage brain tumor (glioblastoma) patient achieved complete tumor disappearance after treatment and has been followed for 382 days as of publication; another end-stage colorectal cancer patient saw the tumor marker CEA decline significantly after the first dose, with tumor shrinkage of 72.8% after three months.
Liu Chu-Chi's tone was notably persuasive when describing the brain tumor patient's current condition: "He was originally bedridden. Now he can get up and go to work. After more than a year of follow-up, the tumor has completely disappeared."
Safety data was equally impressive: none of the 15 patients experienced Grade 2 or higher cytokine release syndrome (CRS), immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS), or graft-versus-host disease (GvHD). Liu Chu-Chi added that the team had originally expected more severe side effects but only observed mild fever in practice.
CAR001's core technology lies in using γδ T cells to enable allogeneic application. Liu Chu-Chi explained: "These cells do not cause rejection, but they account for a very low proportion of our T cells — roughly 1% to 10%. Ever Supreme's technology can amplify the non-rejecting portion to over 98.2%, while reducing the rejecting αβ T cells to below 0.014." Combined with HLA-G targeting and bispecific antibody design, CAR001 simultaneously possesses three key attributes: allogeneic, solid tumor, and low cost.
Competitive Landscape and Licensing Expectations: Starting from a $1 Billion Benchmark
Management specifically highlighted the global competitive landscape for allogeneic solid tumor CAR-T in the presentation. Currently, only one Chinese company has an autologous solid tumor CAR-T on the market, while there are only four players in allogeneic solid tumor CAR-T: Ever Supreme, one Singapore-based company, and two U.S. companies — the latter three are all still in preclinical or Phase I stages, with Ever Supreme being the furthest along.
On licensing valuation, Liu Chu-Chi cited the $1 billion CAR-T licensing deal that
Novartis
granted
Legend Biotech
in 2023 as an anchor, stating bluntly: "Ever Supreme can not only treat solid tumors but also manufacture using allogeneic cells. I believe our technology transfer fee should be worth more than $1 billion."
General Manager
Huang Wen-Liang
added specific timing judgment during Q&A: "Several major international pharmaceutical companies are currently in contact. They prefer to see safety data and efficacy results. After Phase IIa is completed next year, there is a greater chance of initiating substantive licensing negotiations within the following 1-2 years." He also revealed strategic restraint: "The longer we wait before moving downstream, the better the negotiation value may be — but we also need to balance funding needs."
Exosome Dual Track: dEV-001 to File IND Next Year, EXO-001 in Preclinical Hot Zone
The exosome platform was the second major theme of this earnings call. The targeted exosome drug
dEV-001
(Parkinson's disease) has completed animal studies and held a pre-IND meeting with the U.S. FDA, with plans to file an IND and initiate Phase I/IIa in 2027. Liu Chu-Chi explained the core logic of its encapsulation technology: "The blood-brain barrier allows less than 0.1% of antibody drugs to penetrate, and increasing dosage causes cerebral edema or hemorrhage. Exosomes are only 30 to 150 nanometers, and Ever Supreme has attached a targeting head to them, enabling precise delivery to dopaminergic neurons."
Citing WHO data, he noted that the number of Parkinson's disease patients has more than doubled over the past 25 years, with a market size of at least $10 billion projected by 2035. In animal studies, mice in the high-dose group performed significantly better than both the disease control and low-dose groups in running tests, with results published in the
Journal of Nanobiotechnology
.
Another pipeline candidate,
EXO-001
(in-vivo CAR-T), remains preclinical, but Liu Chu-Chi emphasized its strategic position using recent transaction data: between March 2025 and April 2026, six in-vivo CAR-T-related licensing deals occurred globally; in April 2026,
Eli Lilly
acquired Kolon Tissue for $7 billion, a landmark transaction in this space. Liu Chu-Chi stated that EXO-001 animal studies have already demonstrated dose-dependent anti-tumor efficacy, and the company will compile data to apply for a pre-IND meeting with the U.S. FDA.
CDMO Cash Flow Engine: July Revenue Hits Record High, Regenerative Medicine Act a Structural Tailwind
The latter portion of the presentation returned to the CDMO business, with Liu Chu-Chi describing Ever Supreme's operating model as "dual engines": "Contract manufacturing provides cash flow to support new drug R&D, moving forward steadily." July revenue reached NT$100 million (approximately $3.1 million), up 20.7% year-over-year, a monthly record, while Q2 2026 revenue was NT$270 million (approximately $8.5 million), up 22.1% year-over-year.
Liu Chu-Chi addressed the impact of the Regenerative Medicine Act on the CDMO business with a three-tier assessment: existing case types under the Special Regulations can continue; compassionate use can generate additional revenue for products like CAR001 (three patients have already been treated); and after Phase II completion, a five-year provisional drug approval can be applied for. However, he also acknowledged limitations: "Expansion of autologous cell therapy under the Special Regulations is essentially unlikely. The future will inevitably move toward allogeneic cells, so we must transition to the Regenerative Medicine Act framework."
International Expansion: AABB Accreditation Secured, Shuinan GMP Facility to Complete Next Year
Ever Supreme has passed
American Association of Blood Banks (AABB)
accreditation, ensuring product manufacturing and QA/QC meet U.S. standards. Liu Chu-Chi positioned this as preparatory work for licensing and overseas contract manufacturing: "This will facilitate smooth integration for future technology transfers and overseas manufacturing partnerships."
On capacity, the GMP facility in Shuinan is expected to be completed in 2027 to support CAR001 Phase IIb and subsequent commercial-scale production. A North American subsidiary has been established to handle overseas clinical trials for
UMSC01
(umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cells); the Southeast Asian market is planned for expansion through turnkey plant export models for CDMO services.
Q&A Highlights: Gross Margin Concerns, Licensing Timeline, CDMO Ceiling
On-site questions focused on three areas. On gross margin,
CFO Li Po-Chun
responded with data: "This year, whether quarterly or first-half, figures are up compared to the same period last year. H1 is 78%, Q2 is 77%, while last year both quarterly and H1 were 72% — so I'm not entirely sure what the investor is referring to." The chairman added that public hesitation during the Special Regulations-to-Regenerative Medicine Act transition has subsided, with recent business clearly rebounding.
On licensing timeline, Huang Wen-Liang set clear milestones: substantive negotiations within 1-2 years after Phase IIa data is released. He emphasized: "Several major international pharmaceutical companies remain in contact. They want to see efficacy data." For in-vivo CAR-T, the company will accelerate the IND filing after completing the pre-IND meeting and receiving FDA recommendations.
The CDMO growth ceiling was the third focus. Liu Chu-Chi pointed directly to the institutional structure: "The spirit of the Regenerative Medicine Act differs from the Special Regulations. The Special Regulations use autologous cells — as long as foreign literature proves efficacy, the government essentially lets you proceed. But the Regenerative Medicine Act moves toward allogeneic cells, requiring clinical trial proof of efficacy — however, completing Phase II grants a five-year provisional drug approval, which significantly alleviates funding pressure for biotech companies."

Drugs & Therapies.url_match_title: UAE approves new use of drug to treat vitiligo - thenationalnews.com
Drugs & Therapies.content: The UAE has approved the use of a new treatment for non-segmental vitiligo. The Emirates Drug Establishment announced on Monday that the UAE is the first country in the world to adopt the use of the drug, known as Rinvoq, for this purpose. Vitiligo is a condition which causes loss of skin colour in patches. It causes the loss of pigment cells, often resulting in discoloured patches on parts of the body. There is no cure for the disorder, which affects between 0.5 and 1 per cent of the world's population. “The UAE is the first country in the world to adopt the expanded use of Rinvoq, reflecting its advanced position in keeping pace with the latest pharmaceutical innovations and accelerating their availability,” the EDE said. Rinvoq is already approved for use by health authorities in locations including the US and Europe for conditions such as chronic autoimmune and inflammatory conditions. Dr Rekha Santosh, specialist in Dermatology and Aesthetic at Burjeel Hospital, Abu Dhabi, said the approval was "an important development" as the options for people with more extensive cases of the disease have remained limited. "In my practice, I see patients across different age groups whose vitiligo affects visible areas such as the face, hands and neck, and many of them come after trying topical treatments, phototherapy, or combinations of therapies with varying results," she said. "The emotional impact can also be significant, especially for adolescents and young adults. Having a once-daily oral treatment creates an additional option for appropriately selected patients who require systemic therapy. "The oral route can also be advantageous for patients with widespread involvement, where applying topical medication over large areas may be difficult or impractical. "This approval is especially meaningful because it expands the treatment pathway beyond localised therapies. It also reinforces the UAE’s commitment to early access to medical innovation. For many patients, that could be life-changing clinically.”

Drugs & Therapies.content:
Bristol-Myers Squibb US0897961004 Aquarell New Yorker Skyline beleuchtet durch Abenddämmerung mit goldenen Straßenreflexionen, Illustration mit AI erstellt.
Bristol Myers Squibb (ISIN US0897961004) stock is trading in the low $60s in mid-August 2026, with recent data showing a closing price of $63.83 on August 14, 2026, and a modest one-day decline of 1.25% in that latest session per the TradingKey overview
recent quote data
. As of that date, the company’s market value is reported at around $130 billion, underscoring its scale as a large-cap pharmaceutical group within the global healthcare sector per the MarketScreener multi-company snapshot
valuation context
. Investors are now digesting an FDA approval and analyst earnings revisions that together frame the next phase of the company’s oncology and hematology strategy.
Fresh FDA approval in multiple myeloma
One of the key recent catalysts for Bristol Myers Squibb is the regulatory progress for its multiple myeloma franchise, where a new drug has been cleared as the first medicine in an emerging class of cereblon E3 ligase modulators, often referred to as CELMoDs, according to a healthcare technology and digital health weekly overview dated August 17, 2026
digital health report
. In a separate pharma and biotech sector summary published the same day, the company is also credited with securing FDA accelerated approval for iberdomide, another multiple myeloma treatment that marks the debut of a novel drug class, with the report citing recent specialist coverage
pharma sector report
. Taken together, these approvals highlight Bristol Myers Squibb’s push to extend the longevity of its hematology portfolio as legacy therapies face generic erosion and competitive pressure.
For investors, the significance of a first-in-class approval goes beyond the immediate patient population. When a company gains an accelerated approval for an innovative oncology drug, it often signals a path toward confirmatory trials that can convert the label into a full approval and potentially broaden usage. In this case, Bristol Myers Squibb is seeking to translate mechanistic differentiation into commercial traction in a disease area where multiple lines of therapy and combination regimens are common. The new CELMoD-class drug and iberdomide will likely be compared in practice to established proteasome inhibitors and immunomodulatory agents that currently dominate the multiple myeloma landscape, and their ultimate revenue contribution will depend on durability of response, safety profile, and how treatment guidelines evolve over the next few years.
Analyst earnings estimates and consensus valuation
Alongside the regulatory news, several equity research updates compiled on August 17, 2026 point to a constructive longer-term earnings trajectory for Bristol Myers Squibb. A same-day alert on consensus data notes that the company holds a rating profile described as “Moderate Buy” with an average target price of $66.06 per share, placing the implied upside at a small premium to the recent price in the low $60s
earnings estimate alert
. That spread between the average target and the latest $63.83 quote is modest but still indicates that the analyst community generally expects some appreciation as the pipeline and new launches mature.
Another analysis published August 16, 2026 applies a proprietary intrinsic value framework to Bristol Myers Squibb and concludes that the stock trades above that model’s fair value line. In that valuation piece, GF Value is set at $56.48 per share, while the actual market price cited for the company is $63.83, implying the stock is 13 percent above the intrinsic value estimate
valuation analysis
. Put differently, the recent share price sits $7.35 higher than the GF Value calculation, which the commentary characterizes as modest overvaluation rather than an extreme disconnect. For fundamental investors, such a gap raises the question of whether incremental upside will be driven more by earnings growth and pipeline conversion than by multiple expansion from current levels.
Institutional activity also reflects continued interest in the name, even as some funds adjust their exposure. Filings summarized on August 17, 2026 highlight that one investment manager has taken or increased a position in Bristol Myers Squibb while another has trimmed holdings, with each update again referencing the same average target price of $66.06 and the “Moderate Buy” consensus profile
institutional purchase summary
. The pattern suggests that while the stock is not universally embraced, it remains within the buy-rated range for a broad group of analysts and continues to feature in diversified healthcare portfolios, supported by its mix of legacy cash-generating products and newer growth drivers.
Stock price context and recent performance
From a technical and pricing perspective, Bristol Myers Squibb’s recent performance shows the shares consolidating in a relatively tight band close to both the quoted spot price and the multi-company comparison levels. A multi-firm valuation table published August 17, 2026 lists Bristol Myers Squibb at a price point of $63.83 with a one-day percentage move of negative 1.27 percent and a five-day percentage change of negative 1.38 percent, alongside a market capitalization figure of $130 billion that underlines its weight in global indices
comparative valuation table
. Relative to the average analyst target of $66.06, that $63.83 quote leaves a gap of $2.23, suggesting that recent trading levels are within only a few percent of consensus fair value estimates.
A detailed dividend and event timeline for Bristol Myers Squibb compiled by a market data portal provides another perspective on trading behavior. In that overview, the close on August 14, 2026 is again logged at $63.83, with a absolute change of negative $0.81 on the day and a one-day percentage decline of 1.25 percent, while the year-to-date performance at that time shows a gain of 0.53 percent when expressed in euros for a CBOE quotation at 55.96 EUR
dividend and split history page
. For investors comparing the stock to broader indices, a single-digit year-to-date percentage move and a price sitting only a few dollars below the consensus target describe a relatively steady profile, neither sharply discounted nor fully reflecting the potential of its latest pipeline approvals.
Short-term traders may focus on the relationship between daily price moves and news flow, such as the mention of Bristol Myers Squibb in a broader article that discusses strategic pressures at another large pharmaceutical company following a decision to halt a cancer drug trial
sector newsletter
. While that piece centers on a peer, the reference to a potential tie-up involving Bristol Myers Squibb shows how merger speculation can periodically influence sentiment in large-cap pharma even without concrete transaction terms. At the same time, the more tangible drivers for this company appear to be its own approvals, manufacturing investments, and earnings profile rather than unconfirmed transaction scenarios.
Manufacturing expansion and long-term footprint
Beyond clinical and financial metrics, Bristol Myers Squibb is also investing in its physical manufacturing infrastructure in the United States. A news report captured on August 17, 2026 describes the company’s plan to build a new campus with an investment figure of $2.3 billion, aimed at advancing its domestic manufacturing capabilities for future therapies
manufacturing investment report
. The size of this capital commitment signals an intention to align production capacity with anticipated demand from the pipeline and existing portfolio, including complex biologics that require specialized facilities and quality systems.
For long-term shareholders, such a multi-billion-dollar project adds another layer to the company’s growth narrative, complementing the first-in-class oncology approvals. A larger, modern manufacturing base can support scale-up of new therapies and reduce supply bottlenecks, though it also introduces near-term capital expenditure that must be balanced against free cash flow and dividend priorities. The campus plan fits within a broader industry trend where major pharmaceutical companies shore up regional supply chains and reduce reliance on outsourced production, particularly for therapies that form the backbone of critical care and chronic disease management.
Revlimid as a cornerstone multiple myeloma product
Within Bristol Myers Squibb’s portfolio, one of the most recognizable hematology products is Revlimid, a lenalidomide-based therapy that has played a central role in multiple myeloma treatment regimens for many years. As a representative product, Revlimid illustrates how the company built a franchise in blood cancers that later expanded through additional agents and mechanisms, including the new CELMoD-class therapy and iberdomide highlighted in recent sector reports
multiple myeloma pipeline context
. Historically, Revlimid generated multibillion-dollar annual revenue during its exclusivity period, and even as generic competition has entered the market, it remains an important reference point for evaluating newer therapies in this disease area.
The strategic rationale behind developing first-in-class CELMoD agents and securing accelerated approvals becomes clearer when viewed against Revlimid’s lifecycle. As generic erosion gradually reduces revenue from the older product, the company seeks to replace and extend that stream with next-generation drugs that offer differentiated efficacy or tolerability. When investors compare safety and efficacy data from CELMoDs and iberdomide to historical outcomes with Revlimid, they are effectively assessing whether the new agents can not only defend but expand Bristol Myers Squibb’s share of the multiple myeloma market in an environment of rising competition from other large pharmaceutical and biotechnology firms.
Stock level and investor takeaway
Based on recent market data snapshots, Bristol Myers Squibb stock last closed at $63.83 on August 14, 2026, with that quote serving as the most recent full-session price point available in the compiled data from US trading venues
US quote snapshot
. Against an average analyst target of $66.06 and an intrinsic value model point of $56.48 per share, the stock currently trades in a band where expectations for incremental earnings growth and successful commercialization of new therapies are already partly reflected in the valuation but still leave room for debate between value-oriented and growth-oriented investors. For now, the combination of a $130 billion market capitalization, a pipeline that includes first-in-class multiple myeloma drugs, and continued investment in US manufacturing puts Bristol Myers Squibb in a position where execution on upcoming trials and launches will play a central role in determining whether that low-$60s trading range persists or shifts over the coming quarters.

Bristol-Myers Squibb US1078421011 Aquarell des Pharma-Hauptquartiers vor der New Yorker Skyline bei Sonnenuntergang, Illustration mit AI erstellt.
Bristol-Myers Squibb (US1078421011) stock closed at $63.83 on August 14, 2026, as investors digested fresh regulatory wins in multiple myeloma and evolving earnings expectations for the coming years. Recent sector reports as of August 17, 2026 highlight accelerated FDA approvals that expand the companys oncology franchise and help frame the stocks valuation in the mid-$60s.
Share price, valuation and analyst expectations
According to a detailed quote overview
from TradingKey
, Bristol-Myers Squibb shares last traded at $63.83 at the close on August 14, 2026, down 1.25 percent on the day. The same overview shows a 12-month low of $42.52 and a 12-month high of $68.10, placing the latest price closer to the upper end of that trading range, which underscores how sentiment has improved compared with the lows reported earlier in the year.
Market data compiled in a sector snapshot
by MarketScreener
indicates that Bristol-Myers Squibb is valued at about $130 billion at a share price of $63.83, which implies that the company trades at a substantial large-cap premium within global pharmaceuticals. A separate valuation review
from GuruFocus
calculates an intrinsic value of $56.48 per share for BMY versus the recent market price of $63.83, suggesting that the stock is 13.0 percent above this particular fair-value estimate based on its GF Value model.
Consensus forecasts referenced in several institutional holding reports
on MarketBeat
point to an expected full-year 2026 earnings per share of $6.95. That compares with the companys own FY 2026 guidance range of $6.75 to $7.00 per share, indicating that analyst expectations are aligned toward the midpoint to upper half of managements range and reinforcing the narrative of moderate earnings growth.
Recent earnings performance and guidance
The most recent detailed quarterly figures in the institutional summary
from MarketBeat
highlight a strong prior earnings beat that still shapes perceptions of the companys profit profile. In that earlier period, Bristol-Myers Squibb reported earnings per share of $2.04, which exceeded consensus estimates of $1.60 by $0.44, and generated revenue of $12.97 billion compared with expectations of $11.74 billion, a positive gap of $1.23 billion.
Those results represented revenue growth of 5.7 percent versus the same quarter a year earlier, while earnings per share rose from $1.46 in the prior-year quarter to $2.04, a gain of $0.58 per share. The same recap notes that Bristol-Myers Squibb delivered a net margin of 18.87 percent and return on equity of 66.90 percent in that historical quarter, underlining the companys ability to convert its global drug portfolio into cash-generative profits.
Looking ahead, the company has issued full-year 2026 guidance of $6.75 to $7.00 in earnings per share, with the analyst community centered on a forecast of $6.95 per share for the same year
as summarized in a MarketBeat research note
. This tight range, in which the high end of guidance is only $0.25 per share above the low end, suggests that management has a reasonably clear view of near-term profitability, while the modest upside of analyst estimates versus intrinsic-value models illustrates the debate around valuation.
Consensus rating and institutional positioning
Multiple institutional-filings summaries
compiled by MarketBeat
emphasize that Bristol-Myers Squibb currently carries a consensus rating of Moderate Buy, with an average 12-month price target of $66.06. This target sits roughly $2.23 above the recent closing price of $63.83, signaling that the average analyst sees room for single-digit percentage upside rather than a dramatic re-rating.
The same series of reports
from MarketBeat
also highlight active institutional trading in BMY, with some asset managers increasing positions and others trimming exposure as they balance the stocks defensive attributes against valuation questions. An ownership analysis
from TradingKey
notes that as of the first quarter of 2026, 4,176 institutions collectively held 84.35 percent of Bristol-Myers Squibb shares, reinforcing the stocks status as an institutionally dominated blue chip within healthcare.
This deep institutional base, combined with a consensus Moderate Buy stance and a clustered price-target range around the mid-$60s, means that large investors are focusing on execution against guidance and the pace of new drug launches as the primary drivers of incremental returns, rather than betting on a major rerating of the valuation multiple.
FDA approvals expand multiple myeloma portfolio
Sector research summaries
from OriginBrief
highlight that the FDA recently granted accelerated approval to a Bristol-Myers Squibb drug identified as iberdomide for relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma, with coverage on August 14, 2026. The same report describes iberdomide as the first medicine in a novel drug class for multiple myeloma, which represents a strategic extension of the companys long-standing leadership in hematologic malignancies.
An additional healthcare innovation roundup
from OriginBrief
notes that a Bristol-Myers Squibb therapy branded as Zenbexus received FDA approval as the first drug in a new class of cancer medicines called CELMoDs for multiple myeloma, reported in mid-August 2026. While naming conventions differ between sources, the key takeaway is that regulators have endorsed a new generation of targeted molecules intended to improve outcomes in heavily pretreated myeloma patients.
For investors, this wave of regulatory decisions matters because multiple myeloma has historically been a significant revenue contributor for the company through earlier agents, and the extension into CELMoD and related mechanisms can help offset patent expiries and pricing pressure in older oncology products. Combined with the companys existing hematology platform, these approvals could support revenue growth beyond the 5.7 percent quarterly increase recorded in the historical earnings comparison and help justify earnings-per-share guidance in the high-$6 range for 2026.
Competitive and legal context
Within the broader oncology landscape, a newsletter
from Bloomberg
dated August 17, 2026 highlights that another major pharmaceutical company recently halted a cancer drug trial, intensifying investor scrutiny of late-stage oncology pipelines. That development has indirect relevance for Bristol-Myers Squibb, because setbacks at competitors can either open commercial white space in specific indications or raise questions about the risk profile of similar mechanisms across the sector.
At the same time, the valuation note
from GuruFocus
references a lawsuit with a potential financial impact sized at $6.7 billion, which is part of the narrative used to justify a modest overvaluation relative to the GF Value estimate. While litigation outcomes remain uncertain, the scale of the alleged exposure is material when compared with the companys quarterly revenue of $12.97 billion in the historical period and helps explain why some valuation models embed a discount to the prevailing market price.
Together, these competitive and legal factors mean that the upside from new multiple myeloma approvals coexists with headline risk around pipeline execution and legal contingencies. For long-term holders, the balance between these forces will influence whether the stock can sustainably trade above the $66.06 consensus target or converges closer to intrinsic-value estimates in the mid-$50s.
Flagship multiple myeloma therapies
Within its hematology portfolio, Bristol-Myers Squibb has built a multi-pronged approach to treating multiple myeloma that spans traditional agents and newer targeted therapies. The recent FDA accelerated approval for iberdomide, as cited in the August 17, 2026 sector summary
from OriginBrief
, adds a further pillar aimed at patients whose disease has relapsed or become refractory after prior lines of therapy.
In parallel, the approval highlighted for Zenbexus in the healthcare innovation roundup
from OriginBrief
underscores the companys ambition in CELMoD technology, which is designed to modulate the cereblon E3 ligase complex and promote targeted protein degradation in malignant cells. These agents complement existing backbone regimens and can be combined or sequenced to expand treatment options for patients.
For Bristol-Myers Squibb, success in multiple myeloma is strategically important because it can deliver meaningful incremental revenue while leveraging existing commercial infrastructure and medical expertise. If CELMoD-based therapies and other novel agents gain share in relapsed and refractory settings, they can help drive future quarterly revenue growth above the 5.7 percent pace recorded in the historical comparison and support earnings-per-share delivery within or above the indicated $6.75 to $7.00 range for 2026.
Bristol-Myers Squibb stock and current market view
As of the close on August 14, 2026, Bristol-Myers Squibb stock changed hands at $63.83 on the New York Stock Exchange
according to TradingKey
, with the price sitting between the 12-month low of $42.52 and the 12-month high of $68.10 reported in the same data set. Combined with an estimated market capitalization of $130 billion from the MarketScreener comparison
excerpt
, the latest quote reflects how investors are assigning a sizeable premium to the companys pipeline and cash flows despite legal and competitive uncertainties.
With consensus earnings expectations of $6.95 per share for 2026, the recent share price of $63.83 implies a forward price-to-earnings ratio of roughly 9.2 times, which sits modestly above the intrinsic-value estimate of $56.48 per share from the GF Value framework but still compares favorably with many faster-growing but higher-multiple peers. For shareholders, the key questions now are whether the multiple myeloma approvals and ongoing execution can sustain revenue and profit growth at or above the 5.7 percent historical rate while navigating litigation and sector competition.
Read more
More on Bristol-Myers Squibb stock
Key oncology franchise example
One of the most representative elements of Bristol-Myers Squibbs business model is its broad oncology franchise, which includes immuno-oncology, hematology, and targeted therapies aimed at solid tumors and blood cancers. The recent regulatory approvals for novel multiple myeloma agents, as detailed in the August 2026 sector summaries
from OriginBrief
, illustrate how the company seeks to continually refresh this portfolio with new mechanisms such as CELMoDs.
By investing in multiple modalities and indications, Bristol-Myers Squibb aims to create a diversified oncology revenue stream that can help balance the impact of upcoming patent expirations in earlier generations of drugs. For patients, this translates into a wider array of treatment choices and combinations, while for the company it provides a path to maintaining or expanding the net margin of 18.87 percent and sustaining double-digit returns on equity reported in historical periods when new therapies succeed commercially.
NYSE listing and recent price level
Bristol-Myers Squibb stock trades on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker BMY. Based on the latest available quote snapshot
from TradingKey
, the shares closed at $63.83 on August 14, 2026, with a daily decline of 1.25 percent, while remaining within the 12-month range of $42.52 to $68.10. This places the current level somewhat below the consensus target of $66.06, but modestly above the intrinsic-value estimate of $56.48 discussed in valuation models, and highlights how the market is weighing strong cash generation and new drug approvals against legal and competitive overhangs.

Drugs & Therapies.url_match_title: JW Pharmaceutical files phase 3 IND for biweekly obesity drug bofanglutide - koreabiomed.com
Drugs & Therapies.content:
JW Pharmaceutical said Tuesday that it has submitted an investigational new drug (IND) application to the Ministry of Food and Drug Safety (MFDS) for a phase 3 clinical trial of bofanglutide, its investigational obesity treatment, as it seeks to advance the drug in Korea.
JW Pharmaceutical’s headquarters office in Gwacheon, Gyeonggi Province (Courtesy of JW Pharmaceutical)
The trial will enroll 300 adults with obesity or who are overweight in Korea and will evaluate the superiority and safety of bofanglutide compared with placebo through March 2029. The company plans to begin the study in December.
Bofanglutide is a GLP-1 receptor agonist for which JW Pharmaceutical secured exclusive development and commercialization rights in Korea from China’s Gan & Lee Pharmaceuticals in April.
The drug acts on GLP-1 receptors in the pancreas to promote insulin secretion and delay gastric emptying. This increases satiety and suppresses appetite to promote weight loss.
Unlike currently available once-weekly GLP-1-based obesity treatments, bofanglutide is being developed as a subcutaneous injection administered once every two weeks. This dosing schedule could cut injections from 52 to 26 per year, improving treatment adherence and convenience for patients.
The drug has also demonstrated efficacy in previous clinical trials. For example, in the phase 3 GRADUAL-1 study conducted in China, bofanglutide produced significant reductions in body weight from baseline after 52 weeks, with weight losses of 15.12 percent in the 24 mg group and 18.54 percent in the 48 mg group. The study also demonstrated favorable clinical efficacy and tolerability.
JW Pharmaceutical said it plans to sequentially pursue additional phase 3 trials of bofanglutide for indications beyond obesity as part of efforts to strengthen its portfolio of original prescription medicines in the metabolic disease field.
“We plan to clearly demonstrate in Korean patients the strong weight-loss efficacy and tolerability of bofanglutide that were confirmed in previous overseas clinical trials,” a JW Pharmaceutical official said. “We will accelerate development to provide a new obesity treatment option that combines clinical efficacy with greater dosing convenience.”

Drugs & Therapies.url_match_title: EyePoint shares plummet after phase 3 stumble for AMD drug-device combo Duravyu - Fierce Pharma
Drugs & Therapies.content:
EyePoint’s stock was down more than 70% Monday after its experimental treatment for wet age-related macular degeneration (wAMD) missed its key goal in the first of two phase 3 readouts slated for this year.
The pharma is testing its drug-device combo, Duravyu, against Regeneron’s Eylea
(aflibercept), the current standard of care for wAMD and an enduring blockbuster that grossed $4.4 billion in U.S. sales in 2025. But in results published Monday, EyePoint turned to an ad hoc analysis in an effort to salvage the tyrosine kinase inhibitor’s (TKI’s) performance in a phase 3 trial, in which Duravyu
performed worse
than the established treatment on a primary endpoint around best-corrected visual acuity (BVCA) at 52 and 56 weeks.
Based on EyePoint’s press release, the major falter appears to be vision loss that was not caused by wAMD.
Nine patients out of a cohort of 211 on Duravyu, or approximately 4%, experienced vision loss unrelated to wAMD over the course of the trial. But there was no such vision loss in the Eylea arm, a finding that Eyepoint CEO Jay Duker, M.D., called “highly unusual” given historical rates of 3% to 5% non-wAMD vision loss in past phase 3 trials, including those for Eylea. The company says these nine patients confounded the trial results, and when removed in an ad hoc analysis, Duravyu proved its non-inferiority to Eylea.
Related
EyePoint scopes out new commercial chief to prepare for Duravyu launch
EyePoint’s aim with Duravyu is to offer vision benefits equal to those of anti-VEGFs like Eylea while potentially providing more durable delivery. In place of anti-VEGF injections, Duravyu’s ocular implant delivers the drug vorolanib in a sustained-release manner for at least six months, intended to give patients longer-lasting and more continuous relief.
The phase 3 misstep could undercut EyePoint’s ambition to displace Eylea as the high-value treatment of choice for wAMD, a leading cause of blindness in adults over 50, while putting significant pressure on the company’s identical Lucia trial expected to read out this fall.
But several analysts remain confident that a stronger performance in the second late-stage readout could redeem the company’s chances.
This is not EyePoint’s first run-in with disappointment, either. The treatment has been tested in a range of ophthalmology conditions. While it’s had successes with wAMD and diabetic macular edema (DME), the drug
missed the mark
in a study of patients with nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR) in 2024.
Related
EyePoint reports midstage trial fail for Duravyu, raising serious questions about the prospect
While the findings may represent a strike against the drug’s potential approval, Citi analyst Yigal Nochomovitz said “extremely bad luck” may be a legitimate cause of the study’s poor outcome.
“There is precedent in ophthalmology for one failed trial and one successful trial to be sufficient for approval,” Nochomovitz said in an Aug. 17 note. “While we reflect higher LUCIA risk, we see a possible path forward in wAMD.”
And on secondary endpoints, Duravyu was strong. The TKI medicine exceeded expectations by decreasing injection burden by 42%, equating to two fewer injections on average compared to patients on Eylea. Duravyu also showed a strong safety profile and high supplement-free rates.
William Blair analysists said all the data together still suggest Duravyu offers “clinical benefit,” adding in a note that “one clean positive readout” could be enough to see EyePoint through its FDA green light. The fallout from today’s results, however, has bolstered shares of
competitor Ocular
Therapeutix by as much as 11% Monday.
Experts appear to agree that the future of Duravyu is now complicated but not finished. The good news: If it was bad luck, that kind of asymmetry is unlikely to repeat itself in another trial. But some questions must now be answered, namely, what is behind the non-wAMD vision loss. For that, all eyes are on Lucia.
As EyePoint fights to make its case for Duravyu in the indication, Eylea’s reign in the category is being challenged. The anti-VEGF injection was approved for wAMD in 2011 and became an almost immediate blockbuster. While the drug still pulls its weight at Regeneron, biosimilars are crowding out the market. This year, the drug's quarterly sales dropped below $1 billion for the first time in eight years.

Drugs & Therapies.url_match_title: BioNxt Provides Development, Intellectual Property and Commercial Update Across Sublingual Drug Delivery Pipeline - financialcontent.com
Drugs & Therapies.content:
VANCOUVER, BC /
ACCESS Newswire
/ August 17, 2026 /
BioNxt Solutions Inc. ("BioNxt" or the "Company") (CSE:BNXT)(OTCQB:BNXTF)(FSE:BXT), a bioscience innovator specializing in advanced drug delivery systems, is pleased to provide a comprehensive update on the progress of its proprietary sublingual thin-film drug delivery pipeline. The Company continues to advance multiple pharmaceutical development programs, including Cladribine for multiple sclerosis, autoimmune disease expansion, Everolimus and Semaglutide, while strengthening the intellectual property portfolio supporting its platform and preparing for the next phase of clinical and commercial development.
"Our vision has always been to build a differentiated pharmaceutical platform capable of improving the delivery of established therapies across multiple high-value therapeutic areas,"
said Hugh Rogers, Chief Executive Officer of BioNxt Solutions.
"During the past several months we have continued executing against that strategy through scientific development, manufacturing preparation, intellectual property expansion and pipeline diversification. We believe these achievements position BioNxt for an important next stage of growth as we advance toward clinical evaluation and future commercialization."
Cladribine Program Advancing Toward Clinical Development
BioNxt's lead program remains its proprietary sublingual Cladribine oral dissolvable film ("ODF") for the treatment of multiple sclerosis (MS).
Over the past several months, the Company has continued advancing activities supporting the transition from pharmaceutical development into clinical execution. Current activities include regulatory documentation, analytical and manufacturing preparation, and planning for the Company's first human bioavailability study.
BioNxt believes its proprietary sublingual formulation has the potential to improve patient convenience by providing a needle-free, orally dissolving dosage form while leveraging the established therapeutic profile of Cladribine.
The Company also continues evaluating strategic commercialization opportunities and discussions with potential development and licensing partners to maximize the long-term value of the program.
Expanding Opportunities in Autoimmune Diseases
Building upon the Cladribine platform, BioNxt continues evaluating additional autoimmune indications where its proprietary drug delivery technology may provide meaningful clinical and commercial advantages.
The Company's intellectual property portfolio supports potential applications beyond multiple sclerosis, including Myasthenia Gravis and other autoimmune neurological disorders. BioNxt continues assessing future development priorities and regulatory pathways for these additional indications.
Everolimus Program Progress
BioNxt continues advancing formulation development for its proprietary sublingual Everolimus ODF program.
Everolimus is an established pharmaceutical used in organ transplantation and oncology and has attracted increasing scientific interest for potential applications in longevity and healthy ageing research. The Company continues optimizing formulation characteristics while evaluating future preclinical and clinical development pathways.
Semaglutide Program Initiated
BioNxt has initiated development of its proprietary sublingual Semaglutide ODF program, expanding its platform into one of the world's fastest-growing pharmaceutical markets.
The active pharmaceutical ingredient (API) has been ordered, and development activities are being prepared to commence upon receipt. Initial work will focus on formulation development and evaluating the suitability of BioNxt's proprietary thin-film platform for peptide-based therapeutics.
The program represents an important strategic expansion of the Company's platform into metabolic disease and GLP-1 therapies.
Strengthening Global Intellectual Property
BioNxt continues strengthening the intellectual property foundation supporting its proprietary drug delivery platform.
The Company has secured patent protection for its core Cladribine thin-film technology in both Europe and Eurasia, representing the culmination of several years of scientific research, formulation development and intellectual property strategy. These patent grants establish an important foundation for future clinical development, commercial partnerships and licensing opportunities.
In the United States, the Company's corresponding patent application continues under the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office's Track One Prioritized Examination program, which is intended to accelerate examination and final disposition. Additional patent applications continue progressing through examination in other key international jurisdictions.
BioNxt believes a robust international patent portfolio is fundamental to maximizing the commercial potential of both its lead Cladribine program and future pipeline assets developed using its proprietary sublingual drug delivery platform.
Building a Diversified Pharmaceutical Pipeline
BioNxt continues executing a disciplined development strategy focused on advancing multiple proprietary pharmaceutical programs through formulation, manufacturing, regulatory preparation and clinical development.
By leveraging a common sublingual thin-film technology platform across multiple therapeutic areas-including neurology, autoimmune diseases, longevity and metabolic disorders-the Company aims to create multiple long-term value creation opportunities while reducing reliance on a single development asset.
The Company expects to provide additional updates as key development, regulatory, intellectual property and commercial milestones are achieved.
About BioNxt Solutions Inc.
BioNxt Solutions Inc. is a bioscience innovator focused on next-generation drug delivery platforms, diagnostic screening systems, and active pharmaceutical ingredient development. Its proprietary platforms include sublingual thin films, transdermal patches, oral tablets, and a new targeted chemotherapy platform designed to deliver cancer drugs more selectively to tumors with the goal of reducing systemic exposure.
With research and development operations in North America and Europe, BioNxt is advancing regulatory approvals and commercialization efforts, primarily focused on European markets. BioNxt is committed to improving healthcare by delivering precise, patient-centric solutions that enhance treatment outcomes worldwide.
BioNxt is listed on the Canadian Securities Exchange: BNXT, OTC Markets: BNXTF and trades in Germany under WKN: A3D1K3. To learn more about BioNxt, please visit

The compound, named cabamiquine, is described as a "new molecule with drug-like properties" that can be administered in a single dose.
Early clinical trials have shown that combination therapy with pironaradine was effective and had a favorable safety profile in adults and adolescents. This opens up opportunities for further research into combination therapy, including among children.
"This is a significant step forward for a compound that has great potential to simplify dosing regimens for the treatment of malaria – a disease that causes hundreds of thousands of deaths each year," said Dr. Beatriz Baragana, a member of the University of Dundee team that discovered cabamiquin.
The study was conducted by the pharmaceutical company Merck as part of the PAMAfrica consortium. It was jointly funded by the EDCTP2 program with support from the European Union and the Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency.

Drugs & Therapies.content:
AstraZeneca Halts Phase III Lung Cancer Trial as Drug Falls Short Against Keytruda
Add to Google Preferred Sources
AstraZeneca has terminated its Phase III eVOLVE-Lung02 trial after an independent monitoring committee determined the bispecific antibody volrustomig combined with chemotherapy was unlikely to outperform Keytruda in patients with PD-L1-negative metastatic non-small cell lung cancer. The study had enrolled 895 participants across 25 countries, and no new safety signals were identified. The setback adds to a series of 2026 clinical disappointments for the drugmaker, including failures involving Wainua, camizestrant, and Ultomiris. However, AstraZeneca simultaneously reported positive results from two other lung cancer programs: Enhertu in HER2-mutant NSCLC and the Tagrisso-Orpathys combination in EGFR-mutated disease. The company maintains its $80 billion revenue target for 2030, while additional volrustomig trials continue in cervical cancer, head and neck cancer, and mesothelioma.
Key Elements
AstraZeneca
volrustomig
Keytruda
MSD
Enhertu
Tagrisso
Orpathys
Daiichi Sankyo
Susan Galbraith
Wainua
Ionis Pharmaceuticals
camizestrant
Ultomiris
AstraZeneca has terminated a late-stage clinical trial for its experimental bispecific antibody volrustomig in metastatic non-small cell lung cancer after an independent monitoring committee concluded the treatment was unlikely to outperform Merck & Co.'s blockbuster immunotherapy Keytruda.
The decision ends the eVOLVE-Lung02 study, which had enrolled 895 participants across 25 countries. The trial evaluated volrustomig combined with chemotherapy as a first-line treatment for patients whose tumors expressed PD-L1 at levels below 50 percent, with the primary analysis focused on those testing negative for the protein.
The Independent Data Monitoring Committee determined during a planned review that the combination was unlikely to meet either of its dual primary endpoints: progression-free survival or overall survival in patients with PD-L1-negative tumors, defined as expression below 1 percent. The comparator arm received Keytruda, known generically as pembrolizumab.
Susan Galbraith, AstraZeneca's executive vice president of oncology hematology R&D, acknowledged the setback in a statement. "We initiated the eVOLVE-Lung02 trial aiming to improve the outcomes for patients whose lung cancers have lower PD-L1 expression and a less durable response to current immunotherapy regimens," she said. "While we are disappointed, we will learn from this trial and are determined to continue pioneering new medicines from our industry-leading pipeline."
No unexpected safety signals emerged from the study. The adverse event profile observed with volrustomig plus chemotherapy was consistent with the established safety data for each individual treatment.
Shares of AstraZeneca (AZN) edged higher on the news, climbing roughly 1 percent during the trading session. The muted market reaction reflected what analysts described as a modest recovery following several challenging weeks for the pharmaceutical manufacturer.
A Year of Clinical Setbacks
The volrustomig failure adds to a string of development disappointments for AstraZeneca in 2026. Earlier this year, the company and partner Ionis Pharmaceuticals announced that Wainua failed to outperform placebo in the Phase III CARDIO-TTRansform study, which targeted a progressive and life-threatening cardiac disorder.
Additional setbacks included a U.S. regulatory rejection of the breast cancer therapy camizestrant, with regulators citing trial design deficiencies, and a late-stage disappointment for the rare disease treatment Ultomiris.
While individual clinical failures are an expected component of pharmaceutical development, the cumulative effect has intensified scrutiny on the company's ability to convert its pipeline investments into commercial successes.
Competing Wins in Lung Cancer
The week nonetheless brought positive news from two other advanced-stage lung cancer programs. AstraZeneca announced favorable results from the DESTINY-Lung04 trial, in which Enhertu — co-developed with Japanese partner Daiichi Sankyo — demonstrated a statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvement in progression-free survival compared with the standard of care in patients with HER2-mutant non-squamous NSCLC.
Enhertu, known generically as trastuzumab deruxtecan, was tested as a first-line treatment against platinum-pemetrexed doublet chemotherapy plus pembrolizumab in patients with unresectable, locally advanced or metastatic disease.
Separately, the Phase III SAFFRON trial showed that combining Tagrisso (osimertinib) with Orpathys (savolitinib) delivered statistically significant improvements in both progression-free survival and overall survival versus doublet platinum-based chemotherapy in patients with EGFR-mutated NSCLC whose tumors exhibited high levels of MET overexpression or amplification and had progressed on prior Tagrisso treatment.
Volrustomig is a bispecific monoclonal antibody designed to simultaneously block two immune checkpoint pathways, PD-1 and CTLA-4, potentially enabling enhanced immune system recognition and destruction of cancer cells. GlobalData analysis projects the drug could reach blockbuster status by 2032 if it succeeds in other indications.
Additional Phase III trials of volrustomig continue as planned in cervical cancer, head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, and mesothelioma.
The Keytruda Shadow
The eVOLVE-Lung02 failure underscores the formidable competitive challenge posed by Keytruda, which has dominated the immuno-oncology market since its approval. The Merck drug was the best-selling medicine globally in 2025, generating $31.7 billion in revenue.
Merck, known as MSD outside the United States and Canada, faces its own looming challenge: global patents protecting Keytruda's market exclusivity expire in 2028. GlobalData forecasts Keytruda sales will continue growing in the near term, reaching $35.5 billion in 2027, before declining to approximately $19 billion by 2031 as biosimilar competition emerges.
Keytruda accounted for roughly 46 percent of Merck's total sales in 2024. To offset the impending revenue cliff, the company has outlined plans to launch 20 new products, many with blockbuster potential, according to CEO Robert Davis at the JP Morgan Healthcare Conference in January 2026.
AstraZeneca maintains its own ambitious target of $80 billion in annual revenue by 2030, a goal the company reiterated despite the recent clinical setbacks. The drugmaker exceeded second-quarter earnings projections earlier this year, driven by strong sales in its oncology and rare disease portfolios, and anticipates launching up to 20 novel medications over the coming years.
Axel Rudolph, chief technical analyst at IG, noted that AstraZeneca's stock has shown recovery indicators, but cautioned that sustained momentum will require positive clinical trial outcomes in the quarters ahead.

Drugs & Therapies.content:
Controversial “copay accumulator programs” allow insurers to double-dip on patient deductibles. Credit: Getty
Anthem Blue Cross Blue Shield
Cancer
Carelon Rx
Co-195
Colorado
Copay Accumulator Program
Deductibles
ERISA
Healthcare
SB 23-195
Prefer us on Google
Joel Looper
18 Aug 2026 - 12:00am
7
mins
On Nov. 19, 2024, I was diagnosed with polycythemia vera, a rare blood cancer. The day was a blur, but I remember my hematologist, Dr. Fadi Haddad at Houston’s MD Anderson Cancer Center, drawing a picture of my pelvic bones on medical paper to explain my body’s blood production. A gene mutation was causing my bones to make too much red blood, he told me. With treatment, I had perhaps 30 years until my marrow started to give out. After that, treatment could offer perhaps five to seven more years. Then acute myeloid leukemia would set in.
That timeline suggested I could live into my 80s — not bad, all things considered. It assumed, however, access to a specialty medication called Jakafi that would cost me about $9,000 per month (you read that right: per
month
). Dr. Haddad suggested that I apply for a copay-assistance card through Incyte, the drug’s manufacturer. The card would pay my insurer for the Jakafi for the first couple months of each year and meet my deductible, after which insurance would kick in. I did, and soon a pill bottle arrived in the mail that delivered extraordinary results.
But America’s byzantine for-profit health system was, it seems, determined to hinder my healing. Specifically, my health insurer insists that the money paid to it by the drug-manufacturer through my copay assistance card doesn’t count toward the minimum cash deductible I have to meet. This is a clear violation of Texas state law.
Jakafi was a miracle drug. Before the drug, my hemoglobin and hematocrit numbers had been so high that every couple weeks, I needed a therapeutic phlebotomy — “bloodletting,” the ancients might have called it. I had terrible night sweats. My spleen and liver were enlarged enough that they could be felt under my skin. With Jakafi, my numbers stabilized, the night sweats disappeared, and the size of my internal organs normalized. Eventually, I even got cleared to play pick-up basketball again.
Best of all, the manufacturer’s copay card helped me reach our out-of-pocket maximum by late January. I say “best of all,” because my health plan has a high deductible and a high out-of-pocket maximum, both of which tend to go up every year. I have a wife and two small children, and it would almost be easier psychologically speaking to forgo treatment than to leave them with a mountain of medical debt. So when I sailed through my first year of treatment without paying a dime for Jakafi, I felt like I’d dodged a bullet. By fall 2025, I rarely thought about my blood cancer at all.
Last March, however, I received a bill from Anthem Blue Cross Blue Shield, my insurer, for $4,793.99 for a 15-day supply of Jakafi. I called them immediately, and they told me that the funds on Incyte’s copay card had been exhausted. Insurance had covered the first two months of medication, the Anthem representative said — which didn’t quite make sense, if I hadn’t met my deductible, but conversations with health reps rarely make sense. I needed to re-enroll for the copay assistance program, Anthem told me.
Incyte representatives, however, assured me that reenrollment happened in January automatically.
They
had covered those months of medication, not Anthem.
Suggested reading
How passwords stole my sanity
By
Michael Lind
I spent more than 15 hours on the phone over the next few weeks talking to an endless series of Anthem agents and employees at Carelon Rx, Anthem’s pharmacy arm. Finally, someone at Carelon Rx mentioned that I was on a “copay accumulator program.” So far as I knew, I had never heard that combination of words uttered before. A quick internet search explained why.
Copay accumulator programs seem to be based on the belief that patients have to pay their portion of their plan’s deductible and out-of-pocket maximum
personally
before insurance covers subsequent medical bills. No stipulation of this sort is likely to turn up in the documents of your health plan. Yet this is the logic of how copay accumulator programs work, and many insurers avail themselves of it.
In my case, Incyte’s copay card had indeed paid for my January and February orders of Jakafi. But because they had placed me in a copay accumulator program, Anthem never applied that money to my deductible or out-of-pocket maximum. They behaved as if that money had never been paid. Which meant I had to come up with the more than $10,000 deductible before insurance would kick in
— or forgo my medication.
However, that internet search turned up another important detail: what Anthem was doing appeared to be illegal. Colorado (where I work), Texas (where I live), and 23 other states have written stronger legislation, outlawing copay accumulator programs entirely.
The Colorado law
, enacted in 2025 and
often called the “Copay Accumulator Bill,”
is a typical example. It requires “health insurers and PBMs to count any amount paid by the patient or on behalf of the patient by another person, including through a cost-sharing assistant program, toward the patient’s annual out-of-pocket limit and any cost-sharing requirement, such as deductibles, under the patient’s health benefit plan.”
The reasons for laws like Colorado’s are clear enough. No matter who pays a patient’s deductible and out-of-pocket max, her insurance company still gets paid. If another party pays an amount equivalent to that patient’s out-of-pocket max and the insurance company then makes the patient pay that amount
again
, it has doubled her out-of-pocket max without telling them.
“That internet search turned up another important detail: what Anthem was doing appeared to be illegal.”
In some states, the use of copay accumulator programs is largely unregulated. Worse still, the novel application of a 52-year-old federal law allows insurance companies to leverage the programs against patients with certain types of health coverage — even in states where the practice is banned.
The Employee Retirement Income Security Act, or ERISA, was originally meant to ensure that employee benefit plans met certain minimum standards nationwide. To do that, Congress crafted ERISA to preempt every state law involving employee benefit plans. The law’s “saving clause” allows states to regulate insurance — but “self-insured” employer plans, in which the employer rather than the insurance company pays for medical claims, do not count as insurance. This distinction allows some health plans to avoid copay accumulator bans even in states that have them.
Thankfully, my employer offers a fully insured health plan, so Colorado’s SB 23-195
does
apply to me. That explains why I received my Jakafi without trouble after the law went into effect Jan. 1, 2025. But by Mar. 3, 2026, when I received the bill for $4,309.96, Anthem had adapted. Its new approach is to delay and obfuscate.
At any rate, that’s the conclusion I had drawn by Mar. 17, when I filed a grievance with Anthem and began a parallel process through our benefits administrator. In my appeal letter, I meticulously exegeted the Colorado law: Anthem had claimed that “CO-195 is not applicable to this member because they live in Texas.” The law says, “a covered person,” I wrote, not “a covered Coloradan.” It says you must “include any amount paid” on my behalf as counting toward my deductible and out-of-pocket maximum. Anything else is “double-dipping” and “exactly what the state’s Copay Accumulator Bill outlawed.”
Therefore, I told them, I should be reimbursed for funds spent after my deductible and out-of-pocket maximum were met — and that happened back in January.
Anthem says they will respond to a grievance or appeal within 30 days. In my case, it took them until May 19, when they finally followed up with our benefits administrator: “We have received confirmation from our team that the Out-of-Pocket (OOP) Limit of $11,000.00 has been fully satisfied,” the letter read.  I thought for a moment that I had won. Then it added a qualifier: “with no overpayment identified on the account.”
No overpayment.
What sort of creative accounting allowed them to come to that conclusion?
I wondered.
In the months since Anthem declined to honor the Incyte copay payments, I’d incurred other medical expenses, which I’d been forced to pay out-of-pocket — I was owed reimbursement for these expenses.
Then I noticed an Excel sheet attached to the email, one probably requested by our benefits administrator and forwarded to me. It included columns titled “Accumulated Amount,” “Running Total,” and “Reason” among others. Each time Anthem processed an order of Jakafi paid for by the drug’s manufacturer, the running total for my out-of-pocket maximum would jump by more than $5,000. But a day or two later, that amount would mysteriously be removed. On Jan. 20, my total was $5,596.25. On Jan. 21, it was $162.11. On Jan. 30, it was back up to $5,596.25 — and on Feb. 4 it was $430.39. Under the “Reason” given for the Jan. 21 and Feb. 4 deductions, Anthem had simply written, “Miscellaneous adjustments.”
I knew very well what “miscellaneous adjustments” kept these Jakafi orders from counting toward my deductible or out-of-pocket maximum. I was
still
on a copay accumulator plan. Anthem had changed nothing. Instead, a hospital visit for my youngest daughter had put us over the $11,000 threshold, meeting our family’s out-of-pocket maximum. That we could pay the hospital’s bill over several years at zero interest was little comfort. The bill should have been Anthem’s to pay — and it was hardly the only one. By my calculation, Anthem still owes me more than $10,000.
Suggested reading
How healthmaxxing saved my life
By
Emily K. Sipiora
If my story were unusual, I could chalk it up to clunky administrative processes or a missed keystroke somewhere. It turns out, however, that one of my coworkers is having the same trouble with Anthem. A member of that coworker’s family suffers from a rare autoimmune disease. She, too, needs expensive medication. That drug’s manufacturer gave them a copay assistance card worth thousands. Anthem absorbed — in my opinion, stole — that money, too. In my small department, Anthem had put two of us on copay assistance programs, thereby absorbing more than $20,000 of money intended for the treatment of people with rare diseases.
The noncompliance of insurance companies with state copay accumulator bans has received little media attention, but the industry has every incentive to skirt the law. Johnson & Johnson
sued
Cigna, another insurer, for $100 million for appropriating the money J&J gave patients to help pay for their medicines — and that is just one drug company and one insurer. Imagine how much money the American insurance industry is making by secretly doubling the deductibles and out-of-pocket maximums of thousands upon thousands of people.
All of which means that it’s high time that something is done. Congress should address the issues being caused by ERISA, and should pass legislation against copay accumulators: a federal version of Colorado’s SB 23-195 would be a good choice. Americans need a blanket requirement that insurance companies accept any and all money paid on behalf of the patient as counting toward a patient’s deductible and out-of-pocket maximum. Patients also urgently need a recourse to defend themselves when companies openly break the law.
Last month Anthem’s pharmacy manager, Carelon Rx, notified me that the insurance company had come to a decision in my case. Their earlier decision that my out-of-pocket maximum had been met in January has been conveniently forgotten. I now owe them $4,793.99, they said. I spent several more hours on the phone, walking through the details of Colorado SB-195 with two more agents. In both cases, they said they could do nothing except initiate another review, one I can only assume will go nowhere.
I neither have $4,793.99 lying around nor the ability to call an organization to the carpet that insures more than a third of Americans. Thousands of other Americans with rare diseases find themselves in similar positions. We are powerless to defend ourselves against the predatory practices of the health insurance industry, and we need help.
Joel Looper is an editor, theologian, and author of
Bonhoeffer’s America
and
Another Gospel
.

Pharma Industry.url_match_title: SGS expands French bioanalytical laboratory to support complex drug development programmes - Manufacturing Chemist
Pharma Industry.content:
SGS has expanded its pharmaceutical bioanalysis capabilities in France with a 500 m
2
extension to its Saint-Benoît laboratory near Poitiers, taking the site's total modernised footprint to nearly 4500 m
2
.
The investment, SGS said in a statement, is intended to increase analytical capacity,
accommodate rising sample volumes
and enable the laboratory to handle increasingly
complex preclinical and clinical development programmes
— achieved using "new technologies with optimised workflows."
The Saint-Benoît site has more than 35 years of experience in pharmaceutical bioanalysis and supports drug developers from preclinical studies through to clinical trials.
Its capabilities include quantifying small molecules, monoclonal antibodies, biologics, ADCs and RNA-based products, alongside pharmacokinetic (PK) and pharmacodynamic (PD) analysis, immunogenicity testing, biomarker assessment and radioimmunoassay.
Supporting increasingly complex drug pipelines
The expansion comes as pharma pipelines are becoming increasingly diverse, with developers working across conventional small molecules as well as biologics and more complex modalities.
Bioanalytical testing generates data needed to understand drug exposure, biological response and potential immune responses during development, making lab capacity and validated analytical methods important to clinical programme timelines.
SGS already operates a global network of bioanalytical labs and says its services cover early regulatory preclinical studies through to Phase I-IV clinical programmes.
Its broader bioanalytical offering includes assay development, method transfer and validation, PK bioanalysis and biomarker testing.
France's National Agency for the Safety of Medicines (ANSM) has previously recognised the company's GLP compliance at its labs.
Automation and academic collaboration
SGS said the expanded site will continue to develop its use of
automation
and
digitalisation
, alongside collaboration with academic partners.
In 2025, SGS and the
University
of
Poitiers
formalised a partnership covering areas including chemistry, bioanalysis and life sciences.
The relationship is intended to support scientific innovation as well as training and development opportunities for future life sciences professionals.
Walid
Elbast
, Director of the Saint-Benoît laboratory, said the investment would enable the site to support larger studies, growing sample volumes and more complex bioanalytical programmes while maintaining data quality and turnaround times.
This expansion marks an important milestone for the Saint-Benoît laboratory and reinforces our commitment to supporting increasingly complex bioanalytical programmes.
"Through our strong ties with local academic and institutional partners, we are also helping to create new opportunities for future scientists in an environment focused on innovation and excellence."
The latest expansion also builds on a previous major investment at the site: SGS completed an 800 m
2
extension in 2021, taking the laboratory to approximately 3900 m
2
at the time.

Pharma Industry.url_match_title: Controversial pharmaceutical company to relocate to Biomedical Campus - varsity.co.uk
Pharma Industry.content:
A new centre will be constructed on the Biomedical Campus to accommodate the move
Ruying Yang for Varsity
by
Jacob Smith
Monday August 17 2026, 1:55pm
Share on Facebook
Share on Twitter
Share via Email
Share on Pinterest
Share on LinkedIn
Share on WhatsApp
Controversial pharmaceutical giant GlaxoSmithKline (GSK) has
announced
plans to relocate its research and development (R&D) centre from Stevenage in Hertfordshire to the Cambridge Biomedical Campus.
The planned move, which
comes
two years after the company first partnered with the University, will relocate an estimated 1,000 members of staff, with a completion date of 2029.
The move will require the construction of a brand new 300,000 square foot R&D centre on the Biomedical Campus, which will see GSK situated alongside industry competitor AstraZeneca, as well as the new Cambridge Children’s Hospital and Cambridge Cancer Hospital.
The company
plans
to invest £400 million over the next three years to support its move to Cambridge, as well as to upgrade its existing R&D laboratories in Ware, Hertfordshire.
GSK has faced several legal issues in the past. Most recently, the company
settled
out of court over claims that its discontinued heartburn drug, Zantac, caused cancer. It paid $2.2 billion (£1.68 billion) in settlement fees to thousands of claimants across the US in 2024.
In 2012, GSK
pled
guilty to drug fraud charges in the US, resulting in the largest medical healthcare settlement in history, for $3 billion (£2.2 billion). In 2014, a Chinese court
found
GSK guilty of bribery, for which they were fined a total of $490 million (£270 million), with some executives being given suspended jail sentences.
Despite these cases, the University
entered
into a five-year collaboration with the pharmaceutical firm in 2024, under which the company received a £50 million investment through the Cambridge-GSK Translational Immunology Collaboration.
Of the move, GSK’s Chief Scientific Officer, Tony Wood,
said
: “Cambridge has built one of the world’s best life sciences ecosystems, with leading universities, hospitals and biotech companies. […] we see this move as a catalyst for faster, bolder medicines discovery by accelerating the science that matters most for GSK’s next wave of medicines.”
On its website, GSK
states
: “The GSK site will feature state-of-the-art, tech-enabled labs and infrastructure to support research in the company’s focus areas of Oncology, Respiratory, Hepatology, Vaccines and HIV.”
Stevenage MP Kevin Bonavaria
told
the BBC that the move was “disappointing news”. He added: “I am also deeply frustrated by the lack of meaningful engagement from GSK before these plans were announced, which has caused unnecessary uncertainty for employees and the wider community.”
READ MORE
Cambridge University partners with scandal hit drug manufacturers
In a press release on the new plans, the University
said
: “The move will deepen flagship GSK partnerships and collaborations such as Cambridge-GSK Translational Immunology Collaboration, Cambridge Immune Ageing, GSK-Teichmann Lab, and GSK’s Clinical Unit at Addenbrooke’s Hospital.”
When approached for comment, GSK
directed
Varsity
to its press release announcing the move.
The University of Cambridge was contacted for comment.
Support
Varsity
Varsity
is the independent newspaper for the University of Cambridge, established in its current form in 1947. In order to maintain our editorial independence, our print newspaper and news website receives no funding from the University of Cambridge or its constituent Colleges.
We are therefore almost entirely reliant on advertising for funding and we expect to have a tough few months and years ahead.
In spite of this situation, we are going to look at inventive ways to look at serving our readership with digital content and of course in print too!
Therefore we are asking our readers, if they wish, to make a donation from as little as £1, to help with our running costs. Many thanks, we hope you can help!
